subject: Cooking
title: Roman Garum: The Ancient Ketchup
description: A micro-lesson that makes Roman Garum: The Ancient Ketchup usable.

hook.text: Romans poured a fermented fish sauce on almost everything they ate. They called it garum.

buildup.text: Fish guts and salt were left to ferment in the sun for months until they liquefied into an amber sauce.

discovery.text: Garum was pure umami — packed with glutamates, just like modern fish sauce or soy sauce.

twist.text: The finest garum cost more than perfume. Factories in Spain exported it across the entire empire.

climax.text: When Rome fell, garum vanished from Europe — but survived in Asia as fish sauce and soy sauce.

punchline.text: Ketchup changes. The craving for umami never does.

details.summary: Garum was a fermented fish sauce that Romans put on everything — the ancient world's universal condiment. Made by fermenting fish intestines in salt for months, it provided umami flavor centuries before the concept was named.
details.whyItMatters: Garum shows that umami has driven human flavor seeking for millennia. This ancient condiment functioned exactly like modern fish sauce, soy sauce, and Worcestershire sauce — revealing a continuous human craving for fermented savory depth.
takeaways: Garum appeared in nearly every Roman recipe as a primary seasoning
Industrial garum production was the Roman Empire's largest food industry
The flavor profile is nearly identical to modern Southeast Asian fish sauce

faq.question: How was garum made? in practice
faq.answer: Fish intestines, blood, and small whole fish were layered with salt in stone vats and left in the sun for 1 to 3 months. Natural enzymes broke down the fish into a clear, golden liquid. The finest grade, garum sociorum, was as expensive as perfume.

faq.question: Why did garum disappear from Western cooking?
faq.answer: After Rome's fall, centralized production and trade networks collapsed. Medieval European cooking shifted toward vinegar, verjuice, and local herbs. But garum's descendants thrive in Asia.
